references.text: The preceding verse states the principle on which verse 11 is built: whoever is faithful in little is also faithful in much. Faithfulness with "unrighteous mammon" is the small test that determines whether one can be entrusted with what is greater and truer ([ref:Luk 16:10|Luke 16:10]).
Verse 12 continues the argument from verse 11 with a parallel contrast: if you have not been faithful with what belongs to another, who will give you what is your own? ([ref:Luk 16:12|Luke 16:12]).

Jesus concludes the passage by stating that no one can serve two masters – one cannot serve both God and mammon. This shows that faithfulness with mammon in verse 11 concerns using earthly wealth in God's service ([ref:Luk 16:13|Luke 16:13]).

In the parable of the minas, the faithful servant is rewarded with authority over ten cities. The principle is the same as in Luke 16:11: faithfulness in small things leads to being entrusted with what is greater and truer ([ref:Luk 19:17|Luke 19:17]).

Matthew's parallel to Luke 16:13 about no one being able to serve two masters, God and mammon, which underscores the context for the question of faithfulness with unrighteous mammon ([ref:Matt 6:24|Matthew 6:24]).

In the parable of the talents, the master says: "You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much." The same principle as in Luke 16:11 – faithfulness in earthly matters qualifies one for what is true and heavenly ([ref:Matt 25:21|Matthew 25:21]).

Paul emphasizes that what is required of stewards is that they prove themselves faithful. Faithfulness in the stewardship of earthly goods is a test of whether one can be entrusted with true, spiritual wealth ([ref:1 Kor 4:2|1 Corinthians 4:2]).

Paul urges the rich to be generous and share with others, so that they store up treasure as a firm foundation for the future. Proper use of earthly wealth leads to what is true riches ([ref:1 Tim 6:17-19|1 Timothy 6:17–19]).
Moses was faithful in all God's house. Faithfulness is the core quality linked to being entrusted with true and eternal riches, as Jesus asks in Luke 16:11 ([ref:Hebr 3:2|Hebrews 3:2]).
Jesus is referred to as "the faithful and true." He himself is the "true" (τὸ ἀληθινόν) that the believer is entrusted with, in contrast to unrighteous mammon ([ref:Åp 3:14|Revelation 3:14]).
